metric_rationale: The metric zeroes in on two critical trial types where Tallying and WADD have strictly opposite preferences. In Trial 1, Option B has more winning features (3 vs 2) but Option A's features are highly valid (0.95+0.90 > 0.60+0.55+0.50). In Trial 8, Option A has more winning features (2 vs 1) but Option B's single winning feature is the most valid (0.95 > 0.60+0.55). The metric computes the proportion of times the subject chooses the Tallying-preferred option on these critical trials. Tallying will yield a high score, while WADD will yield a low score.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Weighted Additive (WADD) model on 'dissociation' trials. On these specific trials (Trial 1 and Trial 2), one option is superior on the two most valid features (favored by WADD), while the other option is superior on the three least valid features (favored by Tallying). WADD agents will consistently score high on this metric (close to 1), whereas Tallying agents will score low (close to 0), producing a large and stable gap between the two theories.

This metric isolates the starkest dissociation trials in the experiment. In trials where one option has the two highest-validity features (e.g., [1,1,0,0,0]) and the other has the three lowest-validity features (e.g., [0,0,1,1,1]), Tallying strongly prefers the latter because it counts 3 positive features versus 2. In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) rule prefers the former because the combined weight of the top two features (0.95 + 0.85 = 1.80) outweighs the bottom three (0.60 + 0.55 + 0.50 = 1.65). By computing the proportion of times the subject chooses the Tallying-favored option on these specific trials, we expect a very high value under the Tallying theory and a very low value under the WADD theory.

This metric focuses on an 'opposition' trial (Trial 1) where WADD and Tallying make diametrically opposite predictions. The option [1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0] is favored by WADD because it possesses the two highest-validity features, yielding a higher weighted sum. However, Tallying favors the competitor [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0] because it wins on more features (3 vs 2). The metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses the WADD-favored option. Under WADD, this value will be close to 1; under Tallying, it will be close to 0.

To maximally discriminate Take-The-Best (TTB) from the Weighted Additive rule (WADD), we can isolate the specific trials where their predictions diverge. TTB makes decisions based solely on the highest-validity discriminating cue, whereas WADD integrates all cues. By dynamically computing each model's deterministic prediction on every trial, we filter the dataset down to only those 'conflict' trials where TTB and WADD choose opposite options. The metric computes the proportion of choices in these conflict trials that align with TTB. Under the TTB theory, this proportion will be near 1.0 (modulo noise), while under WADD it will be near 0.0. This yields an extremely large mean difference and low per-subject variance.

This metric computes the proportion of a subject's choices that align with the deterministic predictions of the Weighted Additive (WADD) model. Because the experimental design heavily features dissociation trials where WADD and Take-The-Best (TTB) predict opposite choices (e.g., one option is favored by the single most valid cue while the other is favored by the sum of several lesser cues), this metric will yield high values for subjects using a compensatory strategy like WADD and very low values for subjects using a non-compensatory strategy like TTB.

By partitioning trials into 'low opposing' (0-1 cues favoring the alternative) and 'high opposing' (3-4 cues favoring the alternative), we isolate the core divergence between the models. TTB ignores all lower-validity cues, predicting an identical match rate across both partitions (difference = 0). PCS dynamically accumulates evidence, predicting a substantial drop in match rate for the 'high opposing' partition. Pooling across multiple trials dramatically reduces binomial variance compared to single-trial contrasts.

This metric calculates the proportion of times a subject chooses the option favored by the simple majority of discriminating cues, specifically on trials where this majority is opposed by the single most valid discriminating cue. Take-The-Best (TTB) is strictly non-compensatory and will virtually never choose the majority option in these trials (only doing so via random noise). Probabilistic Cue Search (PCS), however, evaluates cues probabilistically and will integrate the multiple opposing cues, leading to a significantly higher rate of choosing the majority option.
